- When sentiment is consistently negative over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to account for subsequent mean reversion; reduce forecast peak by 1–2% and add a slight downward slope after the spike.
- If model consistently forecasts lower than true outcome in early days of a 30-day horizon, it may be underestimating sentiment-driven momentum; increase early forecast by 0.5–1.5% relative to recent mean.
- When sentiment is neutral or mildly positive, model often underestimates upward momentum; add 0.3–0.8% to early forecast to capture sentiment-driven acceleration.
- Model frequently underestimates late-period (last 5–7 days) price increases, especially after sentiment turns positive; apply a 0.5–1.0% upward bias to final 5–7 days of forecast.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes followed by recovery, model tends to lag recovery; shift forecast peak forward by 1–3 days and increase magnitude by 0.5–1.5% to align with sentiment momentum.
